newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai markets take finance shake up in stride.
newsitem.headline: Thai markets take finance shake up in stride.

text.p: Thai financial markets on Tuesday rode out news of Monday's major shake up in the finance sector.
The stock market closed 18.50 points or 2.62 percent lower at 688.74 but off the day's low of 681.74, or down 3.55 percent, on late bargain-hunting.
"The index tumbled at the opening this morning because buying orders dried up while many pending sales orders were carried over from yesterday," said Thanawat Patchimkul of Seamico Securities.
The baht remained steady for most of the day without facing any speculative attack and dealers said news of liquidity problems in the finance sector was discounted by the market.

Thai authorities said on Monday that 10 finance companies hit by liquidity crunches needed to raise their capital urgently. They also said banks and finance companies needed to raise their provisioning for bad loans, which were mainly granted to the ailing domestic property sector.

Previously suspended bank and finance stocks, which were allowed to resume trading on Tuesday were thrashed by investors early on and some fell the daily 10 percent limit. But late bargain-hunting pared losses on the bourse, brokers said.

The baht was quoted steady at 25.925/25.935 against the dollar late on Tuesday compared with 25.927/25.932 late in the morning, dealers said. It moved mostly in line with the surging dollar abroad, they added.
"The news was digested well and there was calm in the forex and swap markets," said N. Rajugopalan, Bank of America country treasurer and vice-president.

The shake up in the finance industry was greeted with mixed reviews by analysts. Some said it was positive that authorities had finally owned up to problems in the finance sector despite earlier denials of rumours to that effect.
Others said the credibility of regulators had been affected by the delayed acknowledgement and that the problems would take time to fix.
Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan appealed to banks and finance firms with surplus funds to aid authorities ease liquidity problems of the weaker institutions.
"The central bank is prepared to help but (private) financial institutions should cooperate by opening credit lines themselves," he said.
Banks and finance companies would have to raise a total of 50 billion baht ($1.94 billion) of reserves within two years under the central bank's order to raise provisions for bad loans.
